outcomes.label: Per-student school funding
outcomes.caveat: Other sources place Texas between 42nd and 47th depending on fiscal year and whether construction and pensions are counted. Per-student figures are also pushed around by enrolment growth and local property values, not only by state appropriations.

outcomes.label: Adults without health insurance
outcomes.comparison: roughly double the national rate of 11.3%
outcomes.sourceName: U.S. Census Bureau, via Cover Texas Now
outcomes.caveat: Driven heavily by Texas not expanding Medicaid, which is a decision of the legislature and governor — but also by the state’s share of agricultural and self-employed work, and by federal subsidy rules that Congress sets.

outcomes.label: Children without health insurance
outcomes.comparison: more than double the national rate of 6.0%; nearly a quarter of all uninsured children in the U.S.
outcomes.sourceName: Georgetown Center for Children and Families
outcomes.caveat: Rose from 10.9% in 2022, a 29% increase. Enrolment paperwork after the pandemic coverage unwinding accounts for part of the rise; eligibility rules set in Austin account for part.

outcomes.label: Infant deaths after the 2021 six-week ban
outcomes.value: infant deaths rose 12.9% in the following year
outcomes.comparison: against a 1.8% rise in the rest of the United States
outcomes.caveat: A single-state time-series comparison, not a randomised finding. The authors attribute much of the rise to congenital anomalies diagnosed too late to act on under the ban. This concerns the 2021 law (SB 8 of the 87th), not any bill on this quiz.

outcomes.label: What households pay for electricity
outcomes.comparison: from 11.50¢ in 2020; delivered rates are running 14–19¢ in 2026, and some monthly bills have reached $600–$800
outcomes.caveat: This increase largely predates the data centre build-out. Natural gas prices, transmission construction, population growth and extreme weather all move retail rates. Treat it as what has happened to bills, not as a data centre effect.

outcomes.label: What data centres are forecast to draw
outcomes.value: ≈78 GW of data-centre demand projected by 2030
outcomes.comparison: against an all-time grid peak of 85.5 GW for the whole of Texas (Aug 2023). ERCOT’s own 2024 forecast for the same year was 29.6 GW — it has since more than doubled.
outcomes.sourceName: ERCOT long-term load forecast, via Data Center Dynamics
outcomes.caveat: A forecast built from interconnection requests, not built capacity — developers request far more than they finish, and ERCOT has revised this number sharply upward twice. Who pays for the transmission it needs is the live question, and is what SB 6 and the 2026 PUC actions are about.

outcomes.label: Spending on Operation Lone Star
outcomes.comparison: border security spending went from $800 million in 2018–19 to $6.6 billion in 2024–25; proposed appropriations would take the running total to roughly $18 billion
outcomes.caveat: Deliberately marked neutral. It has funded roughly 45 miles of state-built barrier, over 100 miles of razor wire and busing more than 119,000 people to other cities. Whether that is money well spent is the argument, not a fact this page can settle. Abbott has asked the federal government to reimburse it.

outcomes.label: Voter turnout
outcomes.comparison: behind every state except Hawaii, Oklahoma, Arkansas and West Virginia
outcomes.sourceName: Ballotpedia turnout analysis; U.S. Census Bureau
outcomes.caveat: Rank depends on the denominator: measured against voting-age citizens rather than eligible voters, Census estimates put Texas 2nd lowest at 57.9%. Turnout also tracks how competitive a state is thought to be, not registration law alone.

outcomes.label: Incarceration rate
outcomes.comparison: counting prisons, jails, immigration detention and juvenile facilities; Mississippi is highest, Massachusetts lowest at 96 per 100,000 in prison
outcomes.caveat: Down 18% over the past decade, so the trend runs the other way from the level. Rates vary a lot by which facility types a source counts.

outcomes.label: Job growth
outcomes.value: 132,500 jobs added in 2025 — more than any other state
outcomes.comparison: real GDP grew 4.8% in 2024, above the national rate; at $2.9 trillion Texas would be the world’s 8th largest economy on its own
outcomes.sourceName: Dallas Fed; Bureau of Labor Statistics via Visual Capitalist
outcomes.caveat: First place is in absolute jobs, which partly reflects being the second most populous state. By growth RATE Missouri led 2025 at +1.7%. Job counts also say nothing about pay: Texas has no state minimum wage above the federal $7.25.

outcomes.label: Property tax burden
outcomes.value: 1.245% effective rate — a median bill of $4,108
outcomes.comparison: against a national average rate of 0.888% and a national median bill of $3,211 — and Texas homes are worth less on average ($313,200 vs $360,600)
outcomes.sourceName: ATTOM property tax analysis, via Fox 4
outcomes.caveat: This is the direct trade-off for having no state income tax: schools, cities and counties are funded from local property levies instead. Whether that is the better deal depends on your income and whether you own. Rates also vary widely by county.

outcomes.label: Renters spending too much on rent
outcomes.comparison: of 4.1 million renter households; 23.6% are severely burdened, paying over half their income in rent. Median rent rose 9.1% after inflation while median household income rose 3.1%, to $78,476.
outcomes.sourceName: U.S. Census / American Community Survey, via Texas Tribune
outcomes.caveat: The burden is concentrated: about 90% of renters earning under $30,000 are cost-burdened, against a far lower share of higher earners, so a statewide average understates how hard it lands at the bottom. Rents are also set by local markets and land supply, not by state law alone.

outcomes.label: How much housing is being built
outcomes.value: 74,350 new residential permits in 2025 — more than any state
outcomes.comparison: Houston ranked 1st and Dallas 2nd among all U.S. cities for new permits, with San Antonio 8th and Austin 9th
outcomes.sourceName: Census building permits, via Wealth Enhancement / Consumer Affairs
outcomes.caveat: Permit volume fell about 9% from the previous year. First place is an absolute count, which partly reflects size and population growth. Note the tension with the figure above: leading the country in construction has not stopped affordability worsening faster here than nationally.

outcomes.label: Texans without a broadband connection
outcomes.comparison: either because the infrastructure does not reach them or because they are not subscribed; four of the five least-connected cities in the country are in Texas
outcomes.sourceName: Texas Consumer Association; National Digital Inclusion Alliance
outcomes.caveat: The 9 million figure combines two different problems — no service available, and service available but unaffordable — which need different fixes. The least-connected-cities ranking is from a 2019 analysis and may have moved since.

outcomes.label: Data privacy enforcement
outcomes.comparison: the largest state privacy recovery against Google by any attorney general, plus $1.4 billion from Meta over facial-recognition data in 2024
outcomes.sourceName: Office of the Texas Attorney General
outcomes.caveat: Secured by Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is a candidate in one of the three races here. Settlement size is not the same as consumer benefit — how much reaches Texans, versus the state treasury and outside counsel, is a separate question this figure does not answer.

outcomes.label: Who pays for a lawyer when you cannot afford one
outcomes.value: the state covers about 13% of the cost
outcomes.comparison: counties pay the rest. In 2013 counties spent $189.7 million against the state’s $27.4 million — 14 cents from the state for every county dollar.
outcomes.sourceName: Texas Indigent Defense Commission; Legislative Budget Board
outcomes.caveat: Marked neutral because it describes who bears a cost, not a ranking — whether the state or the county should fund the right to counsel is the argument. Note the dating: the 13% share is FY2020 and the dollar comparison is 2013, so both may have moved. The 13% is state grants offsetting county spending, not a share of total system cost.

outcomes.label: Exonerations
outcomes.value: more than 470 since 1989 — most of any state
outcomes.comparison: 26 in 2024 alone, ahead of Illinois on 20. Texas has also exonerated 18 people from death row, second only to Florida.
outcomes.caveat: Reads two opposite ways and the number cannot tell you which: it may mean more wrongful convictions, or better machinery for catching them. Both are partly true here. 17 of the 26 exonerations in 2024 trace to misconduct by a single Houston narcotics officer. Texas has also executed more people than any state since 1976.

outcomes.label: Firearm death rate
outcomes.comparison: against 28.0 in Mississippi (highest) and 3.7 in Hawaii (lowest)
outcomes.sourceName: Violence Policy Center, from CDC data
outcomes.caveat: Texas has the highest raw count of firearm deaths of any state, which mostly reflects being the second most populous. Per capita it sits in the middle of the states.

incumbents.name: Greg Abbott
acts: Signed or vetoed every bill that reached his desk in that time.
Vetoed 279 bills across those six regular sessions, 28 of them in the 89th.
Vetoed SB 3, the THC ban, which was the Lieutenant Governor’s third-ranked priority bill.
In 2026 directed the PUC and ERCOT to act on how data-centre costs are allocated, and froze new data-centre projects pending a state audit.

incumbents.name: Ken Paxton
acts: Set up a privacy enforcement team in 2024 and recovered $1.375 billion from Google and $1.4 billion from Meta over Texans’ data.
Has no roll-call record overlapping the three House candidates: his last legislative vote was in 2015, before any of them took office.
Was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the Senate.

incumbents.name: Dan Patrick
acts: Presides over the Senate, assigns bills to committees and controls the calendar.
Published a numbered priority-bill list each session — 25 bills in the 89th.
Does not cast a vote except to break a tie, so he has no roll-call record to score.

causalNote: These numbers are where Texas stands, from the sources named. They are not proof that any one vote, bill or official caused them — rankings move on population growth, local property values, federal rules and the economy as well as state law. What is on the record is the outcome, the vote, and who held office. Draw your own line between them.

omissions.why: Published 2024 road-death figures for Texas conflict (1,997 vs 4,150) and could not be reconciled to a primary source.
No outcome measure exists here that is not itself a value judgement.

opponents.name: Dan Patrick
opponents.whyNoVotes: Presides over the Senate rather than voting in the House, so he casts no vote on these bills.
opponents.evidence: priority-bill designations — bills he publicly named as must-pass
opponents.oneSided: Every bill on that list is one he wanted passed, so it can show where he stood on a bill but never how often he would agree with you.

opponents.name: Greg Abbott
opponents.whyNoVotes: Has never served in a legislature, so he has no roll-call record at all.
opponents.evidence: vetoes — bills he killed after they had passed
opponents.oneSided: A governor only vetoes bills he opposes, and letting a bill become law unsigned is not support, so this can never be read as agreement.

opponents.name: Ken Paxton
opponents.whyNoVotes: His last legislative vote was in 2015, before any of the three took office — there is no session they share.
opponents.evidence: nothing that attaches to these bills
opponents.oneSided: Nothing on his record can be joined to a bill in this quiz, so he appears on no question.
